notes.title: Newspaper App
notes.content:
Top-Level Thread

This note snapshots the conceptual direction that emerged while thinking through the newspaper/news aggregation app. The current app is still working against normal RSS feeds, but the more interesting future direction is aggregating from what the owner described as “tier 2 sources.”

Current Framing

The normal RSS feeds are the clean training wheels: predictable structure, known outlets, steady cadence, and a relatively straightforward path from article ingestion to summarization.

The more interesting piece is aggregating news from tier 2 sources: local reporting, trade blogs, agency pages, press releases, primary-source-adjacent sources, niche beat writers, and other sources that may be noisy or incomplete individually but valuable collectively.

The broader goal is not just “AI summaries of articles.” It is closer to taking messy, scattered information and reconstructing a useful, honest account of what happened.

Identity Of The Project

The project has a strong conceptual identity as a kind of de-shitification engine for news. Modern news sources may already be using AI or SEO practices to make articles more manipulative, bloated, clickbaity, or dishonest. The app can use AI and conventional compute in the opposite direction: stripping the article back down into useful information.

A useful metaphor from the conversation: it is like an end-to-end encoding pipeline where the transmitted data is not encrypted, just degraded into shit, and the local machine is trying to decompress it back into useful signal.

Another useful phrase: a bullshit codec. Lossless decompression for the internet.

Important Design Instinct

The owner wants to do as much preprocessing as possible with conventional compute instead of brute forcing everything with LLM calls. This is a key architectural instinct. LLMs should ideally be the expensive final editor or synthesizer, not the first-line sorter for every raw input.

Classic Information Retrieval Direction

The idea of counting word occurrences, removing common words, and comparing article word distributions is not a weird improvised neural network so much as classic information retrieval.

The core concept is TF-IDF:

  • TF: term frequency, or how important a word is within a given article.
  • IDF: inverse document frequency, or how distinctive a word is across the whole corpus.
  • Common words like articles, pronouns, and generic filler terms get removed or heavily downweighted.
  • Distinctive repeated terms become strong signals for what an article is actually about.

Once articles are represented as sparse vectors of weighted terms, they can be compared cheaply with cosine similarity. That gives a non-LLM way to cluster related articles, detect duplicates, or identify articles that are probably about the same event.

Non-LLM Preprocessing Pipeline

  1. Normalize article text.
  2. Remove stopwords.
  3. Stem or lemmatize terms if useful.
  4. Extract named entities separately if possible.
  5. Compute TF-IDF over title plus body.
  6. Represent each article as a sparse vector.
  7. Compare article vectors with cosine similarity.
  8. Cluster articles above a similarity threshold.
  9. Use an LLM only after clustering, to summarize or synthesize the grouped articles.

N-Grams / Phrase Handling

Single-word matching can work, but meaningful phrases are often much better. This points toward using n-grams.

Examples of useful phrase-level signals:

  • white house
  • federal reserve
  • interest rates
  • rate cut
  • school board
  • supreme court

Counting phrases can make clustering much smarter than counting isolated words alone.

Named Entities

Named entities should likely be extracted as their own signal layer. People, companies, government bodies, cities, agencies, teams, courts, bills, products, and organizations can provide high-value clues for grouping articles.

Named entities may also help distinguish articles that share generic topical vocabulary but are not actually about the same event.

Harder Future Shape

The tier 2 aggregation layer is less like “subscribe to feed, summarize article” and more like:

discover → classify → extract claims → dedupe → cluster by event → merge details → preserve provenance → synthesize

This is the likely shape of the real engine behind the app.

Potential Output Goal

The highest-value output may be a synthesized event article that is the union of useful details across many sources. The app should ideally be able to say:

  • Here is the actual event.
  • Here are the facts all sources agree on.
  • Here are the extra details each source adds.
  • Here is what is still uncertain or source-dependent.
  • Here is where each important detail came from.

Architectural North Star

The LLM should not be the whole system. The more durable architecture is conventional information retrieval and clustering first, followed by LLM synthesis only after the app has already narrowed the problem into coherent event clusters.

A rough summary:

TF-IDF + n-grams + cosine similarity + named entities → article/event clusters → LLM synthesis with provenance

Open Questions For Traversal

  • How should tier 2 sources be discovered and classified?
  • What counts as a source worth ingesting?
  • How should the app distinguish duplicate coverage from related-but-different events?
  • What non-LLM entity extraction options are good enough?
  • How much clustering can be done with TF-IDF before embeddings become necessary?
  • When should the app use embeddings instead of or in addition to TF-IDF?
  • How should provenance be stored so generated summaries can cite their component facts?
  • How should uncertainty and disagreement between sources be represented?
  • What should the user-facing output look like: article, briefing, timeline, fact table, or all of the above?

notes.title: Why This Project Should Exist
notes.content:
Purpose

This note captures the justification for the newspaper app as a project. The parent note frames the top-level problem and proposed direction: modern news consumption is degraded by clickbait, SEO sludge, repetition, source fragmentation, and manipulative framing, while useful facts are scattered across many imperfect sources. This child note explains why the project deserves to exist as more than just another RSS reader with summaries.

Core Claim

The project exists in a gap between ordinary RSS readers and institutional media-intelligence systems.

The individual technical pieces are not novel by themselves. RSS ingestion, article parsing, search indexes, TF-IDF, BM25, n-grams, entity extraction, embeddings, clustering, summarization, provenance tracking, and source-quality modeling are all known problems with known bodies of work.

What appears to be underdeveloped is a practical, open-source, self-hosted tool that combines these pieces into an everyday information-consumption system for a normal technically capable person.

The Gap

The existing landscape appears to split into several categories:

Classic RSS Readers

Tools like FreshRSS, Miniflux, NewsBlur, Inoreader, Feedly, and similar systems solve ingestion, subscriptions, folders, filtering, reading, and sometimes search or summaries. They are useful, but they generally stop at the article level.

They do not usually try to reconstruct events across sources, merge partial details, track provenance of claims, represent uncertainty, or generate a coherent synthesized account from multiple overlapping articles.

Research And Open Data Systems

Systems and datasets like GDELT, Media Cloud, and academic work on event detection, clustering, topic modeling, and stream monitoring contain a lot of the serious intellectual lineage behind this idea.

These systems are powerful, but they are generally aimed at researchers, analysts, journalists, political scientists, OSINT users, or institutions. They are not usually designed as a personal daily newspaper replacement for an individual reader.

Commercial Media Intelligence

Commercial products such as corporate media-monitoring, financial news intelligence, PR monitoring, crisis detection, supply-chain risk monitoring, and institutional news-analysis systems likely contain mature versions of parts of this idea.

They exist because the problem is valuable: organizations need to know what is happening, where information came from, what changed, and what matters.

However, these products are generally expensive, closed, institution-focused, and optimized for business workflows rather than personal understanding.

Open-Source AI News Experiments

There are open-source projects that combine RSS, AI summaries, categorization, embeddings, clustering demos, and digest generation. These are adjacent and worth studying.

However, many appear to be wrappers around article-level summarization or relatively thin AI digest generators. They often do not appear to be trying to build a durable personal information engine with event reconstruction, provenance, uncertainty, source modeling, and conventional information retrieval as first-class architectural concerns.

Why This Is Not Just Another AI Summary App

The goal is not simply to ask an LLM to summarize every article.

The more interesting goal is to use conventional compute and information-retrieval techniques to organize the raw material before the LLM is involved. The LLM should ideally be the final synthesizer, not the whole system.

That means the app should eventually be able to:

  • ingest articles from normal feeds and messier tier 2 sources,
  • identify when multiple articles refer to the same underlying event,
  • deduplicate repeated coverage,
  • preserve details that only appear in one or two sources,
  • track which source contributed which claims,
  • identify agreement and disagreement between sources,
  • distinguish high-authority sources from high-detail sources,
  • strip away clickbait and manipulative framing,
  • produce a useful synthesized account of the event.

Project Identity

A useful shorthand is that this is a personal news intelligence engine, not merely a feed reader.

Another useful framing from the conversation is that the app is a bullshit codec: a system for decompressing degraded internet news back into useful information.

The project has a moral center without needing to be grandiose. It is not trying to replace journalism. It is trying to help an individual reader reconstruct useful reality from degraded inputs.

Why Open Source Matters Here

An open-source version matters because the user should be able to inspect and control the system that mediates their understanding of the world.

A closed commercial system may optimize for institutional priorities, engagement, monetization, or opaque ranking. A personal open system can optimize for clarity, provenance, skepticism, and the user’s own source model.

This is especially important because a system that summarizes and ranks information is not neutral. It needs to expose its assumptions and keep the source trail visible.

Why Self-Hosted Matters

Self-hosting fits the project because the system may eventually reflect personal source preferences, reading habits, local priorities, private feeds, and custom evaluation rules.

It also allows the owner to experiment with local models, local indexing, local search, and private annotations without sending everything to a third-party service by default.

Why This Is A Good Project For The Owner

This project sits at the intersection of several durable interests and strengths:

  • systems thinking,
  • information architecture,
  • bullshit detection,
  • source-quality judgment,
  • local AI experimentation,
  • conventional engineering before brute-force AI,
  • building tools to solve personally felt problems.

It also opens a deep learning path. Hueworks has largely discovered its core architecture and is now in refinement and release-polish territory. This newspaper app still has major unexplored territory and can teach search, ranking, clustering, provenance, NLP, summarization, evaluation, source modeling, and the epistemology of information systems.

Working Justification

This project deserves to exist because the everyday open-source world appears to lack a serious middle ground between RSS readers and institutional media-intelligence platforms.

The pieces are known, but the integration around personal information consumption is the opportunity.

The project should therefore be treated as more than a minor feature of a feed reader. It is a candidate for the owner’s next major project: a self-hosted, provenance-aware, event-reconstructing personal newspaper.

notes.title: Research Lineage And Concept Map
notes.content:
Purpose

This note captures the research and systems lineage behind the newspaper app idea. The goal is not to create a formal literature review yet, but to preserve the conceptual map that emerged from the conversation: this project is adjacent to classic information retrieval, early web search, document clustering, entity extraction, media monitoring, and modern LLM synthesis.

Core Framing

The app is not just an RSS reader and not just an AI summarizer. It is closer to a personal information retrieval and event reconstruction system.

The key architectural instinct is to use conventional compute to organize the problem before using an LLM. The LLM should ideally synthesize already-structured evidence rather than act as the first and only reasoning layer over raw article sludge.

Classic Information Retrieval

The immediate technical lineage is classic information retrieval. This includes representing documents as bags of words, weighted vectors, inverted indexes, and ranked matches.

Important concepts:

  • Tokenization: splitting article text into searchable/indexable units.
  • Stopword removal: removing or downweighting common words that carry little topic signal.
  • Stemming / lemmatization: reducing related word forms to a shared base form when useful.
  • Inverted index: mapping terms to the documents that contain them, which is the classic backbone of search engines.
  • TF-IDF: weighting terms by how important they are in one document and how distinctive they are across the corpus.
  • BM25: a stronger classic ranking function descended from probabilistic information retrieval, often better than naive TF-IDF for search.
  • Vector-space model: representing documents as weighted term vectors.
  • Cosine similarity: comparing document vectors to estimate how similar two articles are.

Early Google Lineage

There is a meaningful connection to early Google-era thinking, but with an important distinction.

Early Google was primarily solving retrieval and ranking:

crawl web → parse documents and links → build index → rank pages using text signals plus link structure

The famous early Google insight was that the structure around documents mattered. PageRank used link structure as a signal of importance. Anchor text, titles, URLs, proximity, and other document/context signals helped rank results.

The newspaper app can borrow the general lesson: useful signals are not limited to article text. The context around an article matters too.

Potential analogs:

  • A major national outlet may be high-authority but low-detail.
  • A local article may be low-authority globally but high-detail for a specific event.
  • A press release may have strong provenance but biased framing.
  • A repeated fact across many sources may deserve higher confidence.
  • A unique fact from one source may be valuable but should retain provenance.
  • Source reputation, source type, publication time, article freshness, citation/link relationships, and named entities can all become ranking or confidence signals.

How This Differs From Search

The app is not primarily trying to answer a search query with a ranked list of documents.

It is trying to reconstruct useful reality from a stream of overlapping, degraded, partial, duplicated, or manipulative articles.

Search problem:

query → ranked documents

Newspaper app problem:

article stream → event clusters → extracted claims → provenance → synthesized account

This makes the project closer to event detection and event reconstruction than classic search alone.

Document Clustering

Document clustering is the bridge between RSS ingestion and event synthesis.

Basic flow:

  1. Represent each article as a vector.
  2. Compare articles using a similarity metric.
  3. Group articles that are likely about the same event.
  4. Separate articles that share general topics but are not the same event.
  5. Feed each coherent cluster into later stages.

Candidate signals for clustering:

  • TF-IDF or BM25 terms
  • n-grams and key phrases
  • named entities
  • dates and timestamps
  • locations
  • source type
  • title similarity
  • article body similarity
  • semantic embeddings, if classic methods are insufficient

N-Grams And Phrases

Single words are useful, but phrases often carry far more meaning.

Examples:

  • federal reserve
  • interest rate
  • rate cut
  • white house
  • supreme court
  • school board

N-grams help avoid losing meaning when important concepts are multi-word phrases.

Named Entities

Named entities should likely be treated as a separate signal layer rather than just ordinary words.

Useful entity types:

  • people
  • companies
  • government agencies
  • courts
  • cities and regions
  • countries
  • sports teams
  • products
  • bills, laws, policies, or named programs

Named entities can help distinguish articles that use similar topical vocabulary but are about different underlying events.

Event Detection And Reconstruction

The deeper lineage is event detection: identifying when multiple documents in a stream refer to the same thing happening in the world.

The newspaper app should eventually reason in terms of events, not just articles.

Possible event object fields:

  • event title
  • event summary
  • time window
  • location
  • entities involved
  • source articles
  • agreed facts
  • unique details
  • conflicting claims
  • open questions
  • provenance links for important claims

Provenance As A First-Class Concern

Provenance is one of the key differences between a useful information engine and AI slop.

The app should preserve where details came from, especially when synthesizing across sources. A generated article should not be a magical answer with no source trail. It should be able to support claims with references back to the source articles or extracted claim records.

Important distinction:

  • The app can synthesize prose with an LLM.
  • But the factual substrate should be traceable.

Uncertainty And Disagreement

Normal summaries often flatten uncertainty. This project should preserve uncertainty when sources disagree or when information is only weakly supported.

Useful categories:

  • facts reported by all or most sources
  • facts reported by one source only
  • claims from official sources
  • claims from interested parties
  • details that conflict between sources
  • details that changed over time
  • facts that are plausible but not yet well-supported

Academic And Commercial Relatives

The project is related to systems used in research, media analysis, finance, public relations, OSINT, crisis monitoring, and institutional news intelligence.

Relevant adjacent categories:

  • media monitoring
  • event detection
  • topic detection and tracking
  • document clustering
  • claim extraction
  • knowledge graph construction
  • source credibility modeling
  • news summarization

Examples of adjacent worlds include GDELT, Media Cloud, commercial media intelligence tools, financial-news systems, PR monitoring systems, and academic event-detection work.

Open-Source Gap

The likely gap is not that nobody has solved the pieces. The gap is that there does not appear to be a mature, open-source, self-hosted, everyday-person tool that combines the pieces into a personal newspaper/intelligence engine.

Most open-source personal news tools appear to live closer to:

RSS reader + article summaries

This project is aiming closer to:

source ingestion + retrieval + clustering + event modeling + provenance + synthesis

Near-Term Conceptual Prototype

A useful first prototype should probably stay humble and prove the core loop before trying to solve the whole problem.

existing RSS article corpus → TF-IDF/BM25 vectors → similarity scoring → article clusters → LLM cluster summary

That prototype would answer the first important question: can the app identify related articles and form useful clusters without using an LLM for every judgment?

Longer-Term Pipeline

discover → classify → extract claims → dedupe → cluster by event → merge details → preserve provenance → synthesize

This remains the high-level research path.

Key Research Questions

  • How far can TF-IDF/BM25 and n-grams get before embeddings are needed?
  • What is the right threshold for article similarity?
  • How should event clusters merge, split, and age out over time?
  • How should a system distinguish one continuing story from several related events?
  • What should count as a claim?
  • Should claims be extracted with rules, local models, or larger LLMs?
  • How should source type and source quality affect confidence?
  • How should the system represent uncertainty in the generated output?
  • What UI makes provenance visible without making the app feel like homework?

Working Mental Model

The newspaper app should borrow from search engines, but it is not a search engine. It should borrow from media-intelligence systems, but it is not an institutional dashboard. It should use LLMs, but it should not be an LLM wrapper.

The durable mental model is:

classic IR and clustering create structured evidence; LLMs turn structured evidence into readable synthesis; provenance keeps the synthesis honest.

notes.title: Product Definition and Editorial Model
notes.content:
Product Definition and Editorial Model

Status: Current long-term product definition for the personalized Newspaper expansion. This is a planning and product-specification subtree, not an implementation-progress log.

Purpose

The mature Newspaper App combines two first-class products over one shared ingestion and article system:

  • Reading Feed: the article-centric RSS-style reading product already being completed in the repository.
  • Newspaper: a stable daily edition that clusters multi-source coverage into neutral, provenance-aware newspaper articles.

The goal is not merely AI summaries. It is a personal news-intelligence system that reconstructs useful reality from fragmented, repetitive, biased, manipulative, and differently reliable sources while keeping important factual claims traceable.

Canonical Product Notes

  1. Product Experience and Edition Contract — Reading Feed versus Newspaper, morning delivery, front page, full articles, stable editions, automatic publication, and variable edition length.
  2. Source Configuration, Admission, and Ranking — per-output routing, source/topic weights, singleton behavior, weighted admission, prominence, breadth, evidence independence, and alternative sources.
  3. Editorial Synthesis, Evidence, and Corrections — neutrality, claim roles, scoped primary-source authority, interested-party handling, uncertainty, citations, corrections, and retractions.
  4. Story, Event, Timeline, and Section Model — continuing stories, discrete events, claim/development timelines, daily articles, Story So Far, event/report times, controlled sections, placement, and tags.
  5. Product Decision Ledger and Open Questions — concise settled-decision ledger, remaining product decisions, and the repository handoff boundary.
  6. Outlet and Upstream Processing Domain Model — explicit Outlet, Input Feed, Output Feed, Article Appearance, outlet-wide dedupe, app-owned classification, upstream processing, and the Intake Group migration.

Current Product Contract

  • The canonical Newspaper is a hosted, immutable edition. PDF is deferred vanity/export polish.
  • Email is a lightweight delivery envelope with the date, section availability, lead headlines, and one edition link.
  • Content cutoff and delivery deadline are independently configurable. Delivery is a hard deadline.
  • One or more valid stories publish automatically; zero stories produce a failed run and failure notification.
  • Generation is deterministic from a sealed manifest with no mutable editorial draft.
  • Generation and phase-level duration metrics support schedule tuning.
  • Outlet is the real-world publishing identity, dedupe boundary, Newspaper source-vote unit, and policy scope.
  • Input Feeds are discovery endpoints; Output Feeds group reading content; Article Appearances record discovery.
  • Extraction and classification occur upstream of outputs against the shared article pool.
  • Weights are absolute effective multipliers centered on 1.0, with visible inheritance and overrides.
  • Ordinary nonlocal admission starts at two eligible Outlets and combined weight 2.0; Local and primary-evidence exceptions are explicit.
  • Coverage breadth determines attention; evidentiary independence determines claim confidence.
  • Primary and interested-party sources are authoritative only within the scope of what they actually establish.
  • The main story experience is readable synthesized prose with numbered citations for unique and consequential claims.
  • Continuing stories use a minimal Active/Dormant lifecycle, discrete events, temporal claims, and an optional concise Story So Far.
  • The Newspaper uses an extensive, evolvable controlled taxonomy, one primary placement, and secondary tags; Politics is a tag.
  • Local is a geographic policy family with place-aware relevance and a bounded high-weight singleton exception.
  • Published errors are handled through linked corrections, clarifications, and retractions rather than silent rewrites.

Maintenance Rule

Keep detailed decisions in their canonical child note and keep the decision ledger current. Rewrite superseded sections to current truth. Do not recreate one large mirrored specification in this hub. Before implementation begins, deliberately reconcile this Trilium subtree into forward-looking, AI-agnostic repository planning documents and replace the current expansion boundary with an implementation-ready roadmap.

notes.title: Product Experience and Edition Contract
notes.content:
Product Experience and Edition Contract

Status: Current product decisions. This is a living source note; revise it to current truth rather than appending contradictory updates.

Purpose

This note defines how the mature Newspaper App feels to use: the relationship between the existing Reading Feed and the new Newspaper, the morning delivery experience, the front page, full articles, stable editions, edition length, and automatic publication behavior.

Two Connected Product Experiences

Newspaper

  • Event- and story-centric rather than article-centric.
  • Combines coverage from multiple eligible sources into coherent synthesized articles.
  • Publishes as a stable daily edition.
  • Organizes stories into familiar newspaper sections.
  • Explains what happened, what changed, what remains uncertain, and where important claims came from.
  • Reads as clean newspaper prose rather than a dashboard, bullet-heavy briefing, or intelligence dossier.

Reading Feed

  • Article-centric and conceptually identical to Ian's current RSS use case and the feed functionality already built in the repository.
  • Lets Ian scan headlines and open individual articles that look interesting.
  • Includes singleton reporting that has not become a multi-source event, plus essays, blogs, reviews, commentary, and entertaining pieces whose value is the article itself.
  • Presents the original article or a hosted/extracted reader-mode version instead of forcing everything through synthesis.
  • Remains a first-class half of the mature site rather than temporary scaffolding.

The two experiences share source ingestion, extraction, topic classification, deduplication, and the underlying article corpus. Their output models remain deliberately different. Reading Feed articles may link to Newspaper stories they contributed to, and a singleton article may later become source material for a Newspaper story after broader coverage appears.

Morning Delivery

The intended experience begins when Ian's coffee is ready. The canonical Newspaper is a hosted, immutable daily edition. Email is the delivery mechanism. PDF rendering is deferred as optional polish or a vanity/export feature rather than part of the first Newspaper release.

The email is a lightweight delivery envelope rather than a second rendering of the Newspaper. It should include:

  • The edition date.
  • A compact indication of available sections.
  • Lead headlines.
  • One prominent link to read the hosted edition.

The website remains the only canonical rendering. It supports drill-down, numbered citations, Story So Far, source traversal, correction links, and archives without duplicating that product inside inconsistent email clients.

The edition should let Ian ignore uninteresting stories simply by not opening them. Reading must not feel like task management.

Front-Page Story Unit

Each story on the edition front page contains:

  • A neutral, system-written headline.
  • A compact factual summary in paragraph form.
  • A visible list of sources that covered the event.
  • A clear path to open the full synthesized article.

The source list communicates breadth of coverage. It does not imply that every listed source independently supports every sentence. Claim-level support belongs in citations and provenance. The front page is a clean reading surface, not an evidence dashboard.

Full Article Experience

Opening a story leads first to a longer, coherent newspaper article synthesized from the available reporting. The default experience is paragraph-form prose, not bullet lists, fact tables, or a structured dossier.

The article does not summarize one selected source. It constructs a new account from the factual substrate across the event's source cluster. Deeper evidence remains available without degrading the primary reading experience.

The reading layers are:

  1. Front page: headline, compact summary, and coverage sources.
  2. Story article: readable synthesized newspaper prose.
  3. Evidence and history: numbered citations, exact sources, prior coverage, timeline, and deeper provenance when deliberately opened.

Stable Daily Editions

Each daily edition is a stable artifact. Its reporting window is defined by the interval since the preceding edition, not by what Ian personally read.

  • The system does not track reading history to decide how much backstory to show.
  • Personalization comes from explicit configuration rather than behavioral surveillance or inferred engagement.
  • Old editions remain browsable as an archive.
  • Later developments belong in later editions rather than silently rewriting earlier ones.
  • The stable-artifact model applies to hosted editions, PDFs, or both.

Edition Scheduling and Processing Window

The edition uses two independently configurable scheduled boundaries:

  • Content cutoff: Freeze the eligible input snapshot. Items discovered afterward belong to the next edition.
  • Delivery deadline: Seal the completed edition and send the delivery email.

The gap between cutoff and delivery is an explicit processing window because extraction, clustering, evidence analysis, synthesis, citation validation, and rendering may take substantial time.

Processing duration must be observable so the schedule can be tuned. Useful edition-level and phase-level metrics include:

  • Total generation duration.
  • Duration of eligibility, clustering, classification, evidence extraction, synthesis, citation validation, and rendering.
  • Queue depth and worker concurrency.
  • Story counts entering and surviving each phase.
  • Failure and timeout counts.
  • Median, percentile, worst-case, and trend data across recent editions.
  • Remaining safety margin before delivery.

The UI may recommend an earlier cutoff when recent runs consistently consume too much of the configured window, but the user retains control of both times.

Automatic Publication Contract

The delivery time is a hard deadline, not a target that slips while the system chases completeness.

  • At content cutoff, the system freezes the eligible input snapshot and begins or schedules processing against that snapshot.
  • At delivery deadline, it automatically seals and publishes whatever complete, valid stories are ready.
  • The edition is emailed automatically without waiting for manual review.
  • Broken or half-generated articles do not enter the edition.
  • One failed source, extraction, cluster, or synthesis must not block the entire Newspaper.
  • Omitted work and failures remain clearly visible in the operator interface.
  • Work completed after the deadline rolls into the next edition rather than mutating the sealed artifact.
  • The sealed edition remains immutable.

The minimum successful edition is deliberately simple:

  • One or more completed valid stories: Publish on time regardless of how thin the edition is.
  • Zero completed stories: Record a failed edition run and send a failure notification instead of fabricating, reusing, or emailing an empty Newspaper.

No minimum page count, section count, or subjective “substantial enough” threshold exists. Ian expects a large source universe, so the zero-story boundary should be exceptional while remaining trivial to enforce.

Deterministic, Non-Mutable Generation

An in-progress edition is not a manually editable draft. Mutable clustering, prose, section placement, citations, or story selection would create a second editorial workflow and undermine reproducibility.

Each run is generated from a sealed manifest containing:

  • Eligible Article and extraction revisions.
  • Source policies and effective weights.
  • Taxonomy version.
  • Story/event inputs.
  • Model, prompt, and schema versions.
  • Content cutoff and delivery deadline.
  • Processing implementation versions.

The operator can inspect why an output occurred but cannot manually edit the edition in place. Retries re-execute failed work against the same snapshot. Configuration changes affect future runs. Published errors use the correction, clarification, and retraction process rather than mutation.

Edition Length

The Newspaper has no fixed story count, page count, or target reading length. Its size is derived from what the system discovers happened during the edition window. Quiet days may produce a thin edition; major news days may produce a large one. Empty sections may disappear.

Open Decisions

  • The actual default cutoff, delivery time, and timezone configuration.
  • Whether supplemental editions ever exist for extraordinary late-breaking developments; the default remains next-edition inclusion.
  • Archive navigation and stable LAN URL shape.

notes.title: Source Configuration, Admission, and Ranking
notes.content:
Source Configuration, Admission, and Ranking

Status: Current product decisions. This is a living source note; revise it to current truth rather than appending contradictory updates.

Purpose

This note defines the configured source universe, routing between Reading Feed and Newspaper, source-by-topic policy, weighted story admission, prominence ranking, coverage breadth, evidentiary independence, singleton behavior, and alternative-source direction.

User-Owned Source Universe

Top stories emerge from the sources Ian explicitly configures. The system should not import a hidden global editorial agenda or infer one from reading behavior.

A story becomes prominent when eligible configured sources cover the same underlying event. Prominence is derived primarily from weighted coverage after clustering, while factual confidence is evaluated separately.

Sources Are Independent From Outputs

A configured upstream source exists independently from every output. Source ingestion, generated RSS membership, and Newspaper participation are separate controls.

  1. Ingestion enabled: Whether the app fetches the source.
  2. Generated RSS memberships: Zero, one, or many output RSS feeds that receive eligible articles from the source.
  3. Newspaper enabled and policy: Whether and how the source contributes to Newspaper discovery, admission, ranking, evidence, and sections.

Disabling Newspaper participation does not remove a source from generated RSS outputs. A source can also be Newspaper-only without belonging to any output RSS feed. Output-feed filtering remains independent from Newspaper filtering.

This distinction is especially important for local sources. A source may remain fully visible in configured RSS outputs, including its national coverage, while its Newspaper policy contributes only geographically relevant local reporting.

Configuration Scope and Inheritance

Newspaper trust and policy usually attach to a logical outlet or intake group, while individual input feeds are discovery plumbing that may need narrower exceptions.

Policy inheritance should follow:

  1. Logical outlet or intake-group defaults.
  2. Individual input-feed overrides.
  3. Topic-specific overrides.
  4. Geographic or Local overrides.

The most specific applicable rule wins. Generated RSS output memberships remain a separate many-to-many configuration rather than inheriting from Newspaper policy.

Source Weighting

All new Outlets begin with a base weight of 1.0. Weights are literal relative multipliers:

  • 1.0 contributes one normal source vote.
  • 2.0 contributes twice as much as a default source.
  • 0.5 contributes half as much.

Ian can tune weights manually over time because sources improve, degrade, change staff, or become less useful. Source medium is not a proxy for reliability. Wire service, newspaper, newsletter, blog, press release, and Twitter account describe formats or roles, not inherent quality.

Overrides are absolute effective weights rather than compound multipliers. The policy hierarchy is:

  1. Outlet base weight.
  2. Individual Input Feed override.
  3. Topic override.
  4. Local or locality-specific override.

The most specific applicable override replaces the inherited value. This avoids surprising multiplication chains and keeps admission explainable.

The UI should show the effective weight next to every override, identify where an inherited value came from, show when a more-specific rule supersedes it, and provide a clear reset-to-inheritance action. It may also preview whether the current effective value clears relevant admission thresholds.

For example, Ars Technica may retain a normal base weight, receive a high Technology weight, and exclude or heavily reduce Politics. A trusted local source may receive a Local weight high enough to qualify singleton local coverage.

Automatic reputation changes are not required. A future system may surface evidence such as frequent corrections, excessive repetition, poor extraction, or low original-information yield, but it should suggest changes rather than silently rewrite Ian's trust model.

Singleton Material

If only one outlet covers something, it normally remains in the Reading Feed rather than becoming a synthesized Newspaper story.

Singleton material is not necessarily low quality. It may be niche original reporting, an essay, analysis, blog post, review, entertaining feature, or an early report that later becomes part of a Newspaper story.

Local News Is a Distinct Policy Family

Local is more than a display section. It needs geographic configuration, local-source policies, and different admission economics from national or broad-topic news.

Locality Profile

The user configures relevant geographic layers such as municipality, county, metro area, state, and other places of continuing interest.

A story is locally relevant when it:

  • Occurs within a configured place.
  • Is an action by a government or institution governing that place.
  • Applies specifically to that place.
  • Has a concrete, direct effect on that place.

Local relevance is determined by the event's relationship to a configured place, not by the publisher's location. Publication by a local outlet, an incidental place-name mention, quoting a local resident, generic national impact framing, or syndicated national coverage does not make a story Local.

A federal law applying only to Pennsylvania can qualify as Local for a Pennsylvania locality profile even though Congress enacted it. A nationwide federal law remains US unless it has an additional concrete place-specific effect.

Local Source Policies

A source may be configured as local coverage only for Newspaper participation. Its nonlocal articles remain available in generated RSS output feeds; they are excluded only from Newspaper contribution under that policy.

Sources can have a distinct Local weight in addition to their default and topic weights. Locality-specific overrides may exist when a source is excellent for one municipality or county but weak statewide.

Local Singleton Admission

Local reporting often lacks the multi-outlet breadth expected of national stories. One sufficiently high-weight Local source can therefore qualify a geographically relevant story for Newspaper synthesis when its effective Local weight clears the Local singleton threshold.

A Local singleton article must remain honest about its evidence base. The source stays visible, unique claims receive citations, and the prose must not imply corroboration that does not exist. Primary documents strengthen the story when available but are not mandatory.

Admission Is Weighted and Continuous

A small number of low-weight sources should not automatically make a story publishable. However, low source weights are not a black-and-white exclusion rule. Widespread lower-weight coverage can qualify because absence from favored outlets may reflect their own shared blind spots.

The initial admission paths are:

  1. Normal nonlocal admission: At least two distinct eligible Outlets and a combined effective weight of at least 2.0.
  2. Local singleton admission: One geographically relevant Outlet whose effective Local weight reaches the configured Local threshold.
  3. Primary-evidence exception: One eligible reporting Outlet plus a primary document that directly establishes the core event.

Admission thresholds remain configurable, but 2.0 is the explainable initial default for ordinary nonlocal coverage.

The primary-evidence exception is scoped claim by claim. A court ruling, enacted law, regulatory filing, official vote record, or similar document can directly establish the event. A company denial establishes that the company denied an allegation; it does not act as a second source corroborating the accusation being denied.

Publication is determined by configurable weighted coverage with no mandatory high-trust anchor. Primary evidence can satisfy an admission path only when it actually establishes the core event.

Prominence, Breadth, and Confidence Are Different

  • Coverage breadth: How many distinct outlets or configured sources chose to discuss the story. This affects whether the story matters enough to cover.
  • Weighted prominence: How strongly those sources contribute under Ian's global and topic-specific policies. This affects admission and ordering.
  • Evidentiary independence: How many genuinely independent reporting or evidence chains support a claim. This affects factual confidence, not whether discussion itself is newsworthy.

Twenty low-weight outlets repeating one allegation may make that allegation Newspaper-worthy because it has become widespread and consequential. It does not create twenty independent confirmations. The synthesized article must explain the actual evidence structure.

Duplicates, Syndication, and Repetition

  • Repeated articles from the same source do not multiply that source's contribution.
  • Exact syndication and substantially duplicate copies are collapsed or attributed to their origin.
  • Distinct outlets independently choosing to discuss the same originating report may contribute to coverage breadth and prominence.
  • Those outlets do not create independent factual confirmation when their claims trace to one source.
  • Ranking and article language should remain explainable in terms of both coverage and evidence chains.

Widespread repetition earns attention, not truth.

Primary and Alternative Sources

The Newspaper should weave nontraditional and primary-source-adjacent material into stories when available:

  • Whitelisted trustworthy Twitter accounts.
  • Newsletters.
  • Press releases.
  • Agency pages.
  • Official statements and documents.
  • Local reporting.
  • Trade blogs and niche beat sources.

Primary documents and official statements are not required for a story to publish. When available, they should be included and can provide high-value evidence within the scope they are qualified to establish. They may contribute to admission and support, but their evidentiary meaning is claim-specific and governed by the editorial-evidence model rather than a generic “official equals true” rule.

In the dream version, the system discovers relevant official statements and press releases automatically. This remains a desired direction rather than a settled first-release requirement. A bounded path should associate known entities with curated official channels before attempting unrestricted discovery.

Explainability

The operator should be able to understand why a story qualified and why it ranked where it did, including:

  • Eligible covering sources.
  • Applicable global and topic-specific weights.
  • Duplicate or syndication collapses.
  • Known citation or dependency chains.
  • Combined admission/prominence score.

Open Decisions

  • The permitted UI range and increment for numeric weights.
  • Whether configured sections beyond Local eventually receive threshold overrides.
  • How official documents contribute numerically when they support only part of an event.
  • How source dependencies and syndicated families are detected and represented.
  • The final UI for Outlet defaults, feed overrides, output memberships, topic rules, Local rules, effective weights, and exclusions.
  • How automated official-source discovery is bounded and verified.

notes.title: Editorial Synthesis, Evidence, and Corrections
notes.content:
Editorial Synthesis, Evidence, and Corrections

Status: Current product decisions. This is a living source note; revise it to current truth rather than appending contradictory updates.

Purpose

This note defines the Newspaper's neutrality goal, claim-level evidence model, interested-party handling, uncertainty language, citations, primary-source semantics, and correction/retraction behavior.

Editorial Goal

The product should deliver actual news separated, as far as a transparent evidence-aware system reasonably can, from partisan framing, editorial slant, clickbait, repetition, emotional manipulation, and source fragmentation.

This is not a promise of omniscient or perfectly objective truth. The defensible product promise is to:

  • Separate reported facts from characterization, analysis, and opinion.
  • Compare claims across sources.
  • Prefer and expose primary evidence where available.
  • Remove emotionally loaded and partisan framing from synthesized prose.
  • Preserve real disagreement instead of averaging it into false balance.
  • Preserve uncertainty rather than laundering repetition into confirmation.
  • Keep material claims traceable to supporting sources.

Article Synthesis Rules

The article should:

  • State well-corroborated facts directly and neutrally.
  • Preserve material context needed to understand the development.
  • Represent uncertainty and disagreement honestly in prose.
  • Attribute unique, disputed, weakly supported, or interested-party claims.
  • Remain a readable newspaper article rather than becoming an evidence table.

No Single Generic Trust Weight for Evidence

A source's configured prominence weight cannot also stand in for claim-level truth. Evidence needs several dimensions:

  • Prominence weight: How strongly the configured source affects admission and story ranking.
  • Claim authority: What the source is actually positioned to establish.
  • Independence: Whether the source supplies independent evidence or repeats another source.
  • Interest or stance: Whether the source is an accused party, accuser, government agency, witness, analyst, advocate, or independent reporter.
  • Claim type: Observation, allegation, denial, official action, quotation, interpretation, prediction, measurement, or another explicit category.

These dimensions prevent institutional status, publication volume, or a primary-source label from becoming a crude truth switch.

Primary Sources Are Authoritative Only Within Scope

A primary source can be high-confidence evidence of its own act or statement without being reliable evidence that all of its substantive assertions are true.

  • A court filing strongly establishes what was filed.
  • An agency announcement strongly establishes what the agency announced.
  • A company press release strongly establishes the company's stated position.
  • An official's post strongly establishes that the official made the statement.
  • None automatically proves every assertion contained within the document or statement.

Interested-Party Denial Example

Suppose Company X is accused of wrongdoing, many outlets report evidence supporting the accusation, and Company X issues a denial. The denial is highly reliable evidence that Company X denied the allegation. It is not high-confidence evidence that the allegation is false because Company X is an interested party with a strong incentive to deny it.

A defensible synthesis may say:

Multiple outlets reported allegations that Company X did X, citing the available evidence. Company X denied the allegations in a statement Tuesday.[1] The statement did not independently resolve the disputed claims.

The denial belongs in the article but must not mechanically balance or outweigh accumulated reporting. Conversely, repeated accusations must not be presented as proven merely because many outlets copied one unsupported claim. The article preserves the structure and limitations of the evidence.

Coverage and Confidence

Story prominence and claim confidence are separate:

  • Prominence: How broadly and strongly the event is covered within Ian's eligible configured source universe.
  • Confidence: How strongly a specific claim is supported and through how many genuinely independent evidence chains.

Broad repetition can make uncertainty important enough to cover. It cannot turn uncertainty into confirmation.

The Newspaper should cover consequential uncertain reports as uncertainty rather than withholding them until certainty appears. Appropriate prose may state:

  • The claim originated with a named source.
  • Other outlets repeated the report but did not independently confirm it.
  • Officials have not commented.
  • No primary evidence was available by the edition cutoff.
  • Available accounts conflict.
  • A statement comes from an interested party.
  • Higher-weight sources had not covered or confirmed the claim by cutoff, without treating their silence as dispositive.

Citations and Claim-Level Provenance

Detailed articles contain numbered citations or annotations for unique and consequential claims, followed by a citation list at the bottom.

Citations are especially appropriate for:

  • Claims unique to one source.
  • Disputed or uncertain claims.
  • Claims made by interested parties.
  • Quantitative or unusually specific details.
  • Direct quotations.
  • Official statements and primary documents.
  • Other details a reader may reasonably want to inspect.

A numbered citation may identify multiple independently supporting sources. The citation list should preserve source name, article or document title, publication time, link, and a short evidentiary annotation when useful, such as “original report,” “official statement,” “interested-party denial,” or “not independently confirmed.”

The provenance surfaces remain distinct:

  1. Coverage sources: who discussed the event.
  2. Inline numbered citations: which claims require specific provenance.
  3. Citation list: the exact material and evidentiary role.

Common facts corroborated throughout the cluster need not receive a citation after every sentence. Readability remains a product requirement.

Corrections, Clarifications, and Retractions

Published editions remain artifacts and are never silently rewritten.

Future editions contain a separate Corrections, Clarifications & Retractions section when necessary. Each notice:

  • Identifies and links to the original edition and article.
  • States what was originally reported.
  • States what is now known.
  • Explains whether the change is a correction, clarification, or full retraction.

The original article retains its original content. The hosted archive may display separate metadata or a notice around it indicating that a later correction exists and linking forward. This creates bidirectional linkage without modifying the historical text.

Open Decisions

  • The exact claim-type and source-role vocabulary.
  • How claim authority, independence, interest, and support are represented internally.
  • Whether any user-facing confidence language or indicators appear beyond natural prose and citations.
  • The operator workflow for correcting a bad synthesis, citation, claim relationship, or interested-party classification before publication.
  • The exact correction/retraction operator workflow after publication.

notes.title: Story, Event, Timeline, and Section Model
notes.content:
Story, Event, Timeline, and Section Model

Status: Current high-level product model. This is a living source note; revise it to current truth rather than appending contradictory updates.

Purpose

This note defines continuing stories, discrete events, claim/development timelines, daily edition articles, optional backstory, reader-facing time order, and the controlled section/tag model.

Continuing Story Structure

The system should not allow one article cluster to grow indefinitely. It should distinguish several related layers:

  1. Story thread: A durable continuing subject or unfolding narrative.
  2. Event: A concrete occurrence within that story.
  3. Claim/development timeline: What happened or was alleged, when it happened, when it was first reported, and how its support changed.
  4. Daily edition article: A prose synthesis emphasizing relevant developments since the preceding edition cutoff.
  5. Story So Far: An optional contextual reconstruction from the accumulated history.

For example, “Federal Reserve monetary policy” may be a continuing story thread. A rate decision, press conference, and later inflation report are separate events or developments connected to that thread. The edition synthesizes what is new without collapsing the entire subject into one permanent blob.

Minimal Story Lifecycle

Story lifecycle should remain deliberately simple:

  • Active: The thread has current qualifying developments.
  • Dormant: No qualifying developments have appeared for the configured inactivity period.
  • New related activity automatically returns a dormant thread to Active.
  • No automatic Resolved, Finished, or Closed state is needed.
  • Merge and split operations exist only to correct clustering identity mistakes.

The inactivity duration is an implementation-tuning value rather than a major product concept. Nothing needs to be declared permanently settled before the heat death of the universe.

Later Articles Are Not Assumed to Be Perfect Supersets

Coverage of an unfolding event will often repeat earlier information and add new details. That pattern is useful, but the system must not assume every later article is a reliable superset.

Later articles may:

  • Add genuinely new claims or evidence.
  • Repeat older reporting.
  • Omit prior details.
  • Correct earlier claims.
  • Contradict earlier reporting.
  • Reframe the event without adding information.
  • Lag behind the best-known current state.

The system therefore needs temporal, source-aware claim comparison rather than simple replacement of old articles with newer ones.

Daily Development Article

  • The main article focuses primarily on developments since the preceding edition.
  • It does not retell the entire timeline every morning.
  • It remains understandable without requiring the reader to have read yesterday's edition.
  • Earlier edition articles, the underlying timeline, and evidence remain available for deeper traversal.

The Story So Far

Continuing stories show a collapsed The Story So Far panel beneath the current article:

  • One visible sentence summarizes the necessary prior context.
  • Expanding it reveals a concise prose backstory.
  • The backstory links to relevant prior edition articles and timeline entries.
  • New or genuinely standalone events do not show the panel.
  • The backstory is generated as of the edition cutoff and becomes part of the edition's stable snapshot.

Timeline Semantics

The reader-facing timeline should be ordered primarily by when real-world events happened. Publication and first-report times remain visible as secondary provenance.

Both clocks matter:

  • Event time explains the real-world sequence.
  • Publication or first-report time explains how public knowledge evolved, what was known by an edition cutoff, and whether later articles corrected or merely repeated earlier information.

If event time is unknown, first-known publication time may serve as the provisional ordering signal while uncertainty remains explicit.

Controlled Section Taxonomy

The Newspaper starts with a fairly extensive controlled catalog rather than arbitrary user-created semantics. The initial top-level sections are:

  • World
  • United States
  • Local
  • Business
  • Finance & Markets
  • Technology
  • Science
  • Health
  • Environment & Energy
  • Sports
  • Automotive
  • Arts & Culture
  • Entertainment

The initial controlled cross-cutting tags include:

  • Politics
  • Elections
  • Courts
  • Regulation
  • Economy
  • Labor
  • Education
  • Public Safety
  • National Security
  • Climate
  • Space
  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Gaming
  • Real Estate
  • Media

Politics is deliberately a tag rather than a top-level section. Political stories are placed according to their primary real-world domain or geography—World, United States, Local, Business, Finance, or another section—and tagged Politics plus more specific concepts such as Elections, Courts, or Regulation.

Longform, opinion, lifestyle, food, and travel are initially better treated as Reading Feed categories because they usually describe an article form or interest rather than a cluster of developing events.

Taxonomy Must Be Evolvable

The controlled vocabulary is an initial product vocabulary, not a permanent prison.

  • Sections and tags are durable reference records with stable identifiers rather than enums hard-coded throughout the application.
  • Display name, order, and enabled state are independently configurable.
  • New categories can be introduced without a database schema migration or broad code rewrite.
  • Used categories are retired, aliased, merged, or split rather than destructively deleted.
  • Renames do not break source policies or historical editions.
  • Classifier configuration is generated from the active taxonomy.
  • Published editions snapshot their placement and tags so later taxonomy changes do not rewrite history.

Placement and Tags

Every Newspaper story has:

  • One canonical primary section controlling placement.
  • Any number of secondary controlled tags.
  • One canonical article, never duplicated across multiple sections.

A Federal Reserve decision may be placed in Finance & Markets while carrying tags for Politics, Regulation, Economy, and related concepts. Tags support filtering, navigation, source policy, and topic-specific weighting without padding the edition through duplication.

Local Placement and Geography

Local covers configured municipality, county, metro, state, and other relevant place layers. Stories appear once in Local and carry the matching geographic and topical tags.

The geographic classifier must distinguish events occurring within a place or directly affecting it from stories that merely originate at a local publisher or mention the place incidentally.

Open Decisions

  • The inactivity duration used to move an Active thread to Dormant.
  • The UI and data shape for locality profiles and multiple places of interest.
  • Rules for assigning a primary section when several apply.
  • The minimal automated and operator rules for correcting mistaken event merges or splits.
  • How continuing story threads are initially created and linked.
  • The exact UI for timelines, prior editions, and Story So Far.
  • Future additions, aliases, merges, or splits in the initial section and tag vocabulary.

notes.title: Product Decision Ledger and Open Questions
notes.content:
Product Decision Ledger and Open Questions

Status: Routing summary for settled product decisions and remaining specification work. Detailed rationale lives in the sibling product notes; this note should stay concise and current.

Settled Product Decisions

  1. The mature site has two first-class pieces: the article-centric Reading Feed and the event-centric Newspaper.
  2. Sources exist independently from outputs. Ingestion, zero-to-many generated RSS memberships, and Newspaper participation are separate controls.
  3. Newspaper policy inherits from logical outlet/intake-group defaults through input-feed, topic, and geographic overrides, with the most specific applicable rule winning.
  4. The canonical Newspaper is a hosted daily edition. PDF is deferred as optional vanity/export polish.
  5. Email is a lightweight delivery envelope containing the date, available sections, lead headlines, and one prominent edition link.
  6. The edition uses independently configurable content-cutoff and delivery times because processing may be lengthy.
  7. The delivery time is a hard deadline. The system automatically seals, publishes, and emails completed valid stories without manual review.
  8. Failures do not block successful stories; incomplete work is omitted visibly and late completions roll into the next immutable edition.
  9. Generation duration and phase-level processing metrics are first-class so cutoff and delivery times can be tuned.
  10. Edition length is determined by discovered events, not a fixed story or page count.
  11. The front page uses a neutral headline, compact factual paragraph, and coverage-source list.
  12. The full story is a clean synthesized newspaper article in prose, with evidence available at deeper layers.
  13. Personalization comes from explicit source, topic, weight, geography, and section configuration rather than reading-history tracking.
  14. Sources begin equally weighted and can be tuned globally, by feed, by topic, and for Local coverage over time.
  15. Source medium does not determine reliability; specialist accounts may outweigh institutional outlets for their beats.
  16. Single-source material normally stays in generated RSS Reading Feeds.
  17. Newspaper admission uses configurable weighted coverage with no mandatory high-trust anchor.
  18. A few low-weight sources may fail admission, while sufficiently widespread low-weight coverage can qualify.
  19. Coverage breadth and evidentiary independence are distinct: repetition can make a story important without confirming its claims.
  20. Exact duplicates and syndication collapse, while distinct outlets discussing one report may add prominence but not factual confirmation.
  21. Primary sources are desirable but not required. They are authoritative only within the scope of what they actually establish.
  22. Interested-party statements and denials are included and explicitly classified; they do not mechanically settle disputed substance.
  23. Evidence cannot use one generic trust number. Claim authority, independence, interest/stance, and claim type remain separate from prominence weight.
  24. Consequential uncertainty is covered as uncertainty rather than suppressed or presented as fact.
  25. Unique and consequential claims receive numbered citations with an annotated citation list at the bottom.
  26. Continuing stories contain discrete events and a claim/development timeline rather than one indefinitely growing cluster.
  27. Daily articles emphasize developments since the preceding edition, with optional Story So Far context.
  28. Reader timelines order primarily by event time while retaining publication and first-report time as provenance.
  29. The initial controlled sections are World, United States, Local, Business, Finance & Markets, Technology, Science, Health, Environment & Energy, Sports, Automotive, Arts & Culture, and Entertainment.
  30. Politics is a controlled tag rather than a section. Stories have one primary placement and secondary tags.
  31. The taxonomy uses evolvable stable reference records; later additions, renames, retirements, aliases, merges, and splits must not require broad rewrites or alter historical editions.
  32. Local is a geographic policy family based on an event occurring in or concretely affecting configured places, not on publisher location.
  33. Local-only Newspaper policy does not remove nonlocal articles from generated RSS feeds.
  34. A sufficiently high-weight Local source can qualify a geographically relevant singleton story, with explicit single-source provenance.
  35. Published editions are never silently rewritten. Later corrections, clarifications, and retractions link backward, while archived articles may show non-destructive forward notices.
  36. An edition publishes on time if at least one valid story completes. Zero completed stories create a failed run and failure notification rather than an empty or reused Newspaper.
  37. Edition generation is deterministic from a sealed manifest and has no mutable editorial draft. Inspection and retries are allowed; manual output edits are not.
  38. Weights are literal multipliers centered on 1.0. Overrides are absolute effective values, and the UI displays inheritance and effective weight.
  39. Normal nonlocal admission initially requires two distinct eligible Outlets and combined weight 2.0.
  40. One reporting Outlet plus a primary document can qualify when the document directly establishes the core event.
  41. Story lifecycle uses only Active and Dormant; related activity automatically reactivates the thread.
  42. Continuing stories show one sentence of visible context followed by a collapsed concise Story So Far with prior-edition and timeline links.
  43. The first Newspaper release uses configured RSS/Atom feeds and existing extraction tiers; Twitter, newsletter-specific ingestion, and automated official-source discovery are deferred.
  44. Outlet is a first-class real-world editorial identity, required parent of Input Feeds, outlet-wide dedupe boundary, source-vote unit, and policy scope.
  45. Input Feed is a discovery endpoint; Output Feed is a generated RSS grouping for consumption. Related reading content belongs in Output Feed membership, not a generic intake grouping.
  46. The existing Intake Group concept should semantically migrate to Outlet rather than survive as a separate abstraction.
  47. Article Source should become Article Appearance terminology so feed discovery remains distinct from evidentiary sources and reporting dependencies.
  48. Article classification is app-owned and article-level. Sub-feed membership and upstream categories are preserved as hints, not authoritative taxonomy.
  49. Extraction and classification move upstream of outputs so the enriched article pool exists independently of generated RSS membership.

Remaining Product Specification

  • Choose actual default cutoff, delivery time, timezone controls, and archive URL/navigation behavior.
  • Choose the permitted UI range and increments for source weights.
  • Define how partially supporting primary documents and reporting dependencies affect support metadata.
  • Define the Outlet/Input Feed migration details and app-owned classification artifact model in the repository implementation plan.
  • Choose the minimal Active-to-Dormant inactivity default and cluster-correction behavior.
  • Finalize claim types, source roles, interest relationships, and provenance vocabulary.
  • Define the deterministic correction workflow for errors discovered after publication.
  • Define the first implementation roadmap from Outlet migration and upstream extraction/classification through clustering, synthesis, hosted editions, and delivery.
  • Design the Outlet, feed, source-policy, locality, edition, story, citation, archive, and correction interfaces.

Implementation-Handoff Rule

Before Newspaper implementation begins, reconcile this Trilium product subtree into the repository's AI-agnostic forward-looking planning documents. The first implementation prerequisite is the opinionated Outlet migration plus upstream extraction and classification. Replace the current expansion boundary with an implementation-ready roadmap while preserving the existing generated RSS Reading Feed as a standalone product.

notes.title: Outlet and Upstream Processing Domain Model
notes.content:
Outlet and Upstream Processing Domain Model

Status: Settled product/domain direction for the Newspaper expansion. This is a living source note; revise it to current truth rather than appending contradictory updates.

Why the Model Is Becoming More Opinionated

V1 intentionally used generic intake feeds, optional intake groups, and generated output feeds. That flexibility was useful while proving feed ingestion, deduplication, extraction, digestion, and publishing. The personalized Newspaper now needs explicit real-world concepts for source weighting, coverage breadth, topic policy, evidence provenance, and cross-outlet clustering.

The previous interpretation that intake groups existed to group related content for reading was a miscommunication. Related content should be grouped for consumption through generated output-feed membership. The durable role of the existing intake-group machinery is outlet-wide deduplication across multiple feeds from the same real-world editorial source.

The app should therefore become opinionated at the real domain seams instead of preserving generic abstractions that make every later policy ambiguous.

Canonical Vocabulary

Outlet

An Outlet represents one real-world editorial or publishing identity, such as Reuters, Ars Technica, The Wall Street Journal, a local newspaper, or a local television station.

Outlet is preferred over Publisher because Publisher may later mean a corporate owner such as Hearst, Condé Nast, or News Corp. Corporate ownership and outlet affiliation can be added as separate relationships if they become useful.

An Outlet is:

  • The required logical parent of its normal input feeds.
  • The deduplication boundary across those feeds.
  • The unit counted for Newspaper coverage breadth.
  • The default scope for Newspaper enablement and source weighting.
  • The default scope for topic and Local policies.
  • The durable home for display identity, canonical domains, notes, and future source-quality observations.

Input Feed

An Input Feed is one RSS or Atom discovery endpoint belonging to an Outlet.

It owns transport and endpoint concerns:

  • Feed URL.
  • Fetch enabled state and cadence.
  • HTTP cache validators and last-fetch state.
  • Feed-specific extraction or classification overrides.
  • Raw upstream categories, feed title, and other classification hints.
  • Optional narrower generated RSS membership.

Output Feed

An Output Feed is a generated RSS product used to group content for consumption. Technology, Finance, Automotive, Local, source bundles, and any other user-defined reading group belong here.

Output feeds select whole Outlets and/or individual Input Feeds:

  • Including an Outlet means all current and future enabled feeds belonging to it.
  • Including an individual Input Feed allows precise selection of only part of an Outlet's feed surface.
  • Output membership does not define outlet identity, deduplication, Newspaper eligibility, extraction enrollment, or classification ownership.

Article Appearance

The existing concept currently named Article Source is actually a discovery record: it says that an article appeared through a particular Input Feed and Raw Item.

It should be renamed Article Appearance or Feed Appearance. This preserves an essential distinction:

  • An appearance records where the app discovered a published article.
  • An outlet identifies the publishing/editorial brand.
  • A reporting dependency records that one article relies on another report.
  • A claim citation/source records evidence supporting a synthesized claim.

Using Source for all four concepts would become a semantic tar pit once provenance and claims are first-class.

Canonical Relationship

Outlet
  └── Input Feeds
        └── Raw Item / Article Appearances
              └── Canonical Articles
                    ├── Generated RSS Output Feeds
                    └── Newspaper discovery, clustering, and generation

A canonical Article normally belongs to one publishing Outlet and can have several appearances across that Outlet's feeds. Similar articles published by different Outlets remain distinct canonical Articles and are connected later through cross-outlet event clustering rather than intake deduplication.

Syndication remains a separate provenance problem. A local site may host an AP article: the local brand is the publishing outlet/host, while AP may be the originating reporting source. That dependency should eventually be modeled explicitly rather than corrupting basic article identity.

Intake Group Becomes Outlet

There is no longer a product reason to preserve Intake Group as a separate generic abstraction. Its important existing role—deduplicating related feeds from one source—maps directly to Outlet.

The intended semantic migration is:

  • intake_groups becomes outlets.
  • intake_group_id becomes outlet_id.
  • generated_feed_intake_groups becomes generated_feed_outlets.
  • Group-based deduplication becomes outlet-based deduplication.
  • Previously ungrouped Input Feeds receive an Outlet rather than remaining identity-less.
  • Duplicated outlet-name strings become proper Outlet relationships or deliberate immutable presentation snapshots.
  • ArticleSource and article_sources become Article Appearance terminology.

This migration keeps the useful grouping and deduplication machinery while giving it the domain meaning it should have had. A separate Feed Group or Intake Boundary should only be introduced later if a concrete non-outlet deduplication requirement appears.

Classify Articles Independently

The app should classify extracted canonical Articles against its own controlled taxonomy. It should not treat sub-feed membership or publisher categories as authoritative classification.

Upstream feed metadata remains useful as a cheap and explainable prior:

  • An article discovered in WSJ Technology receives a strong Technology hint.
  • Feed categories, titles, and source tags remain preserved as classification evidence.
  • The app-owned classifier may confirm, add to, or override those hints.
  • Classification produces one primary Newspaper section plus controlled secondary tags.

App-owned classification is necessary because publisher taxonomies are inconsistent, duplicated, liable to drift, and unable to express the source-by-topic and geographic policies already chosen for the Newspaper.

Move Processing Upstream of Outputs

The Newspaper requires a complete enriched article pool that exists independently of generated RSS membership.

Outlet / Input Feed policy
  → fetch
  → canonicalize and deduplicate within Outlet
  → extract once at Article level
  → classify once at Article level
  → shared enriched Article pool
      ├── generated RSS selection and rendering
      └── Newspaper eligibility, clustering, and generation

The first architectural prerequisite for Newspaper work is therefore moving extraction enrollment and later classification upstream from output-feed pipeline steps to Outlet/Input Feed/Article policy.

  • A source can participate only in the Newspaper without fake output-feed membership.
  • Extraction artifacts remain article-level reusable state.
  • Classification artifacts are produced once and reused by all outputs.
  • Generated RSS feeds consume enriched Articles but do not cause those Articles to become eligible for processing.
  • Newspaper clustering operates across the complete eligible article pool.

The current code already stores endpoint fetch state on Input Feeds. The deeper relocation is processing enrollment and ownership: extraction and classification must be upstream domain operations rather than side effects of generated RSS publication.

First Newspaper Input Scope

Before the first Newspaper run, Ian expects to configure many ordinary feeds and organize them under Outlets. This existing ingestion surface is sufficient to create a useful corpus after upstream extraction and classification are available.

The following source classes are explicitly deferred from the first Newspaper release:

  • Twitter-specific ingestion.
  • Newsletter-specific ingestion.
  • Automated official-source discovery.

Configured RSS/Atom feeds plus the existing extraction tiers should first prove weighted admission, clustering, evidence-aware synthesis, hosted editions, and scheduled delivery.

Design Principle

Outlet is who published it and the deduplication boundary. Input Feed is where it was discovered. Output Feed is where the user wants to read it.

Opinionated domain modeling does not reduce useful extensibility. It moves extensibility to the real seams: Outlets, feeds, appearances, articles, events, claims, and outputs each have one clear role.
